intro: This Nepali date converter switches instantly between Bikram Sambat (BS) and Gregorian (AD) dates. It is the fastest way to verify a birth date, fill in citizenship, passport or academic documents, and align the Nepali and English calendars.

Bikram Sambat is Nepal's official calendar, running about 56 years and 8 months ahead of the Gregorian calendar. Because the length of each Nepali month changes from year to year, accurate conversion needs the official calendar tables — which is exactly what this tool uses.

items.q: How many years apart are BS and AD dates?
items.a: Bikram Sambat runs about 56 years 8 months ahead of the Gregorian calendar. For example, AD {{adYear}} corresponds to BS {{bsYear}}. The Nepali new year starts on Baisakh 1 (mid-April).

items.q: How do I convert a Nepali date to English?
items.a: Choose BS → AD mode above and pick the year, month and day — the English date, weekday and full details appear instantly. AD → BS works the same way in reverse.
Conversions are based on the official Nepali calendar month tables, so results are reliable for birth dates, documents and official use.

items.q: How many days are in a Nepali month?
items.a: Nepali months have 29 to 32 days, and the count can differ each year because months are set by the sun's zodiac transition (sankranti).
All commonly used BS/AD years are supported — from historical dates to upcoming years.

intro: The panchanga is the heart of the Vedic calendar — its five limbs (tithi, vara, nakshatra, yoga and karana) describe the religious and astrological character of each day. This page shows today's tithi, moon sign, sunrise–sunset, moonrise and auspicious times in full detail.
Calculations are based on astronomical ephemeris positions, so tithi start and end times are accurate to the minute. Use the daily panchanga to plan fasts, pujas, shraddha and auspicious ceremonies.

items.q: How do I find today's tithi?
items.a: Today's tithi, nakshatra, yoga and karana are shown automatically on this page. A tithi is defined by the sun–moon angular distance, so it can change mid-day; the exact start and end times are listed too.

items.q: What are the five limbs of the panchanga?
items.a: Tithi, vara (weekday), nakshatra, yoga and karana — together these five make up the panchanga, and festivals and auspicious times are set from them.

items.q: What are tithi vriddhi and tithi kshaya?
items.a: When the same tithi spans two sunrises it is vriddhi (repeated); when a tithi touches no sunrise it is kshaya (skipped). This is why the Nepali calendar sometimes repeats or skips a tithi.

items.q: Which location is this panchanga calculated for?
items.a: By default it follows Kathmandu sunrise; if you allow location access, timings adjust to your own city's sunrise and sunset.
A moment is a window when the panchanga limbs align favourably — weddings, bratabandha and house-warming are traditionally timed to it. Abhijit moment and daily sait are available in this patro.

intro: Nepal public holidays {{bsYear}} BS ({{adYear}}) — the complete dated list of festivals and national days including Dashain, Tihar, Chhath, Lhosar, Eid and Christmas. Use it to plan leave, office schedules and travel.
Festivals based on lunar tithis fall on different English dates each year; the dates here follow standard panchanga calculations.

items.a: Dashain (Vijaya Dashami) falls in the bright fortnight of Ashwin — the exact dates this year, from Ghatasthapana to Kojagrat Purnima, are in the list above.

items.q: Which day is the weekly holiday in Nepal?
items.a: Saturday is Nepal's weekly public holiday. Most government offices are open Sunday through Friday.

items.q: Why do festival dates change every year?
items.a: Most Nepali festivals follow lunar tithis — the alignment between tithis and Gregorian dates shifts each year, so the AD date of a festival moves.

items.q: What calculation is this holiday list based on?
items.a: Festival and holiday dates are computed from the standard Kathmandu panchanga, which applies throughout Nepal.

tithi.what: A tithi is a lunar day — one of the 30 phases of the Moon in a lunar month. It is the time the Moon takes to gain 12° of angular separation (elongation) from the Sun.
tithi.how: Computed from the difference between the Moon's and Sun's ecliptic longitudes. Each 12° of that gap is one tithi (30 tithis × 12° = 360°). Because it depends on the Moon's varying speed, a tithi can be shorter or longer than a solar day; the exact begin/end instants are found where the elongation crosses each multiple of 12°.
tithi.meaning: The tithi governs most festivals, fasts (Ekadashi, Purnima, Aaushi) and muhurta selection. Shukla paksha (waxing) tithis 1–15 lead to the full moon; Krishna paksha (waning) tithis 1–15 lead to the new moon.

nakshatra.what: A nakshatra is one of the 27 lunar mansions — equal 13°20′ divisions of the zodiac through which the Moon passes, occupying each for roughly a day.
nakshatra.how: The ecliptic (360°) is divided into 27 equal arcs of 13°20′. After applying the Lahiri ayanamsha, the nakshatra is read from the Moon's sidereal longitude; begin/end times are the instants the Moon crosses each 13°20′ boundary.
nakshatra.meaning: The nakshatra drives the birth star (janma nakshatra), tarabala, and muhurta. Each is ruled by a deity and a planet and carries its own nature (fixed, movable, fierce, and so on).

yoga.what: A (nitya) yoga is one of 27 Sun–Moon combinations. It is not a physical position but a value derived from their combined longitudes.
yoga.how: Add the Sun's and Moon's sidereal longitudes and divide the total (0–360°) into 27 equal parts of 13°20′. Each part is one yoga; begin/end are when the combined longitude crosses each boundary.
yoga.meaning: Some yogas are auspicious (Siddhi, Amrita) and some malefic (Vyatipata, Vaidhriti, the opening of Vishkumbha). Yoga is one of the five limbs of the panchanga checked when choosing a muhurta.

karana.what: A karana is half of a tithi. There are 60 karanas in a lunar month, of 11 distinct types (7 movable that repeat, and 4 fixed).
karana.how: Each tithi (12° of elongation) is split into two 6° halves, and each half is a karana. The 7 movable karanas cycle round, while the 4 fixed karanas are anchored around the new moon (Aaushi).
karana.meaning: Karana refines timing within a tithi. The Vishti (Bhadra) karana is inauspicious for auspicious work; the fixed karanas (Shakuni, Chatushpada, Naga, Kimstughna) are considered heavy.

chandra-rashi.what: The Moon sign is the zodiac sign (rashi) the Moon occupies — one of 12 equal 30° signs. It changes about every 2¼ days.
chandra-rashi.how: From the Moon's sidereal longitude, the rashi is longitude ÷ 30°. Transition times are the moments the Moon crosses each 30° sign boundary.
chandra-rashi.meaning: The Moon sign is the basis of Vedic rashiphal (horoscope), chandrabala, and the janma rashi used in naming and matchmaking.

choghadiya.what: Choghadiya divides the day (sunrise→sunset) and night (sunset→sunrise) into 8 muhurtas each — 16 slots ruled in turn by planets, each marked good, bad, or neutral.
choghadiya.how: Daylight is split into 8 equal parts and night into 8 equal parts, so each part's length varies with the season. The ruling planet of each slot follows a fixed sequence starting from the weekday's lord, and the planet's nature sets the quality.
choghadiya.meaning: A quick, popular muhurta guide for daily tasks and travel — pick a Shubha/Amrita/Labha slot and avoid Roga/Kala/Udvega.

hora.what: Hora is the planetary hour — the 24 hours of a day, each ruled by one of the 7 planets (Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn).
hora.how: Day and night are divided into planetary hours from sunrise. The first hora of the day is ruled by the weekday's lord, then the sequence follows the Chaldean order, each hora advancing by one planet.
hora.meaning: Choose a hora whose ruling planet suits the task (Jupiter for study, Venus for the arts, Mercury for trade), and avoid malefic horas (Saturn, Mars, Sun) for delicate work.

lagna.what: Lagna (the ascendant) is the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a given moment. Over a day all 12 signs rise in turn.
lagna.how: Computed from the local sidereal time and the observer's latitude — the point of the ecliptic crossing the eastern horizon. Each sign's rising duration differs by latitude and by sign (short and long ascension).
lagna.meaning: The lagna is the first house of a chart and the anchor for muhurta and kundali; the sign rising at an event's time shapes its outcome.

udaya-lagna.what: Udaya Lagna lists the exact clock times each ascendant sign rises through the day, and flags the Pushkara Navamsha moments within them.
udaya-lagna.how: The same ascendant maths as Lagna, but presented as a table of rising→setting times for each sign, with the Pushkara navamsha degrees (auspicious sub-divisions) marked where they fall.
udaya-lagna.meaning: Used to pin a muhurta to the exact rising-sign window, and to catch the auspicious Pushkara moments for important beginnings.

chandrabala.what: Chandrabala ("Moon strength") measures how favourable the Moon's current sign is relative to a person's birth Moon sign.
chandrabala.how: Count signs from the birth Moon sign (janma rashi) to the Moon's transit sign. Positions 2, 5, 7, 9, 11 (and others by tradition) are strong and favourable; 1, 3, 6, 10 are weaker — tabulated for each rashi.
chandrabala.meaning: A strong Chandrabala day supports travel, ceremonies and new work; weak Chandrabala warns that rashi to be cautious.

tarabala.what: Tarabala ("star strength") rates the day's nakshatra against a person's birth nakshatra through the nine-tara cycle.
tarabala.how: Count from the birth star to the day's star and take it modulo 9 → one of nine taras (Janma, Sampat, Vipat, Kshema, Pratyari, Sadhaka, Vadha, Mitra, Ati-mitra). Some are auspicious, some to be avoided.
tarabala.meaning: The good taras (Sampat, Kshema, Sadhaka, Mitra, Ati-mitra) favour action; Vipat, Pratyari and Vadha are avoided for important work.

panchaka-rahita.what: Panchaka Rahita shows the windows of the day free of the five "panchaka" faults (Mrityu, Agni, Raja, Chora, Roga) that make certain acts inauspicious.
panchaka-rahita.how: The weekday, tithi, nakshatra and lagna are combined; when their combination lands on one of the five panchaka faults it is flagged. The remaining clear time is "panchaka-rahita" (panchaka-free).
panchaka-rahita.meaning: Choose panchaka-free windows for acts the five faults specifically prohibit — roofing, travelling south, buying fuel or wood, or funerary rites.

pushkara.what: Pushkara Navamsha are especially auspicious sub-segments: specific navamsha (1/9th) divisions within certain nakshatras where the ascendant becomes "Pushkara" (nourishing).
pushkara.how: Each sign's 30° is split into nine 3°20′ navamshas; in defined sign/navamsha pairs the rising point qualifies as Pushkara. The page marks the clock moments the lagna passes through these.
pushkara.meaning: Acts begun in a Pushkara Navamsha moment (purchases, investments, foundations) are held to prosper and multiply.
